# `Q-26-8` — lmd module did not compile

> An `.lmd` module that a cell, filter or shortcode handler required has a Lua syntax error or a markdown fragment that does not parse, so `require` failed. The requiring cell is left as written.

## What this means

`require("name")` found `name.lmd` (an lmd module: Lua with markdown
fragments) and compiled it before loading, and the compile step failed.
The message names the module file and the position inside it; when the
problem is a markdown fragment that does not parse, the reader\'s own
diagnostic for that fragment follows as an info line. The error is
located on the `require` line of the cell, which is left displayed; a
Lua filter or shortcode handler that required the module fails the way
it would for any error in `require`.

## Why this happens

- A Lua syntax error in the module, reported with the module\'s own line
  and column.
- A markdown fragment in the module that the reader rejects, for
  example a bare apostrophe after a word ([`Q-2-10`](../markdown/Q-2-10.qmd)).
- A fragment holding markdown the emitter has no constructor for yet
  ([`Q-26-2`](Q-26-2.qmd)), or an inline fragment that parses to several
  blocks ([`Q-26-3`](Q-26-3.qmd)).

## How to fix

Fix the module file at the position the message names. To see the Lua
a module compiles to, call `quarto.lmd.compile(source, name)` from a
cell, which returns the compiled text or raises this same error.

A module written in lmd is an ordinary Lua chunk otherwise: it returns
its value (by convention a table of functions), and `require` resolves
it relative to the requiring file, then relative to the document.

````markdown
```{lmd}
local cards = require("components/cards")
return cards.card("Hello", {=[ from a module ]=})
```
````

## Related errors

- [`Q-26-1`](Q-26-1.qmd): the same Lua syntax error, in a cell rather than a module.
- [`Q-26-4`](Q-26-4.qmd): the module compiled but raised while running; the message names the module line.
